## Overview

@Konigswieser2020 grew a spruce forest on a grid of square metres, each
holding at most one tree, from a handful of trees to a forest of 9 ha. Trees
age, gain wood, die, and drop saplings near them, more readily when they have
a few neighbours than when they have none or many. The authors used the
forest to ask what contaminated ground, strip harvests, droughts and bark
beetles do to it. Their main finding concerns the beetles: brought into a
young forest, they either die out at once or wipe out nearly all of it, and
the forest then takes well over a century to recover.

This implementation is an **adaptation**. The source gives most of its rules
with numbers but not how far saplings land, how close to other trees they may
grow, the order of events within a year, or exactly how beetles are shared
among trees. These are chosen below, and the first two are calibrated to the
source's growth curve.

```{julia}
#| output: false
ENV["GKSwstype"] = "100"
using EcologicalCellularAutomata
using CellularAutomataCore
using Plots
using Statistics
```

## The model

Each cell holds at most one tree, with an age, a dry wood mass and a number
of bark beetles. Each year:

- Within every cell (the model's rule), a tree ages a year and gains 28 kg of
  wood until it is 70, then 14 kg until it is 140, approaching the source's
  "approximately 3000 kg". It dies with probability 0.05 while it is at most 3
  years old, 0.01 until 150, and 0.2 after that.
- Beetles on a tree multiply tenfold, three times a year, and each time the
  same number is shared equally among the other trees within 10 m. A tree
  carrying 200 beetles or more at the end of the year dies, and its beetles
  with it.
- Every other year each tree drops a sapling, with a probability that depends
  on its neighbours `n` within 10 m: none with no neighbours (no
  pollination), 1/2 with 1 to 3, certainly with 4 to 9, 1/2 with 10 to 50, and
  none with more (no room). The sapling lands in a random cell within 6 m and
  takes root if no tree stands within 2 m of it and at most 50 within 10 m.

Beetles, spreading and harvest act tree by tree, each depending on what was
done before it, so they are a callback stored with the problem. The forest
starts from 20 trees aged 10, within 20 m of the centre of a 300 × 300 grid.

```{julia}
prob = problem(:bark_beetle_forest; seed=1)
keys(prob.u0), prob.tspan
```

The state at time `t` is the forest at the end of year `t`. We record the
standing trees, their wood in tonnes, the wood felled and the trees infested
each year:

```{julia}
function forest(prob; maps=())
    integ = init(prob; save_everystep=false, save_start=false)
    rows = [bark_beetle_counts(integ.u)]
    snapshots = Dict{Int,Matrix{Int}}()
    while integ.t < prob.tspan[2]
        step!(integ)
        push!(rows, bark_beetle_counts(integ.u))
        integ.t in maps && (snapshots[integ.t] = Int.(integ.u.age) .* integ.u.tree)
    end
    return rows, snapshots
end
runs(n; kwargs...) =
    fetch.([Threads.@spawn first(forest(problem(:bark_beetle_forest; seed=s, kwargs...)))
            for s in 1:n])
column(rs, k) = reduce(hcat, [getfield.(r, k) for r in rs])
```

## Calibrating the saplings

The source says only that saplings land "in a certain radius" and "not too
close to other trees", and that its authors tuned the radii by experiment.
Its forest grows along an S-shaped curve: about 4000 to 5000 trees after 100
to 120 years, and about 9900 (1100 a hectare) from year 250. How far saplings
land sets how fast the forest spreads; how close they may grow, with the
limit of 50 neighbours, sets how dense it becomes:

```{julia}
sweep = [(r, d) for d in (1.5, 2.0, 2.3) for r in (4, 6, 10)]
curves = fetch.([Threads.@spawn getfield.(first(forest(problem(:bark_beetle_forest; seed=1,
                     years=250, pmap=(sapling_radius=r, spacing=d)))), :trees)
                 for (r, d) in sweep])
plot(0:250, reduce(hcat, curves); lw=1.5, xlabel="year", ylabel="trees",
     label=permutedims(["within $r m, $d m apart" for (r, d) in sweep]),
     color=permutedims(repeat([1, 2, 3], 3)),
     ls=permutedims(repeat([:dot, :solid, :dash]; inner=3)),
     legend=:outerright, legendfontsize=7, size=(800, 380), left_margin=5Plots.mm,
     bottom_margin=5Plots.mm)
scatter!([110, 250], [4500, 9900]; color=:black, marker=:x, ms=6, label="source")
```

Saplings landing within 6 m and kept 2 m from other trees (the defaults)
follow the source's curve; 1.5 m (no tree in the eight cells around) lets the
forest grow too dense, and 2.3 m keeps it far too sparse.

## The forest without disturbance

Five runs of 300 years, as in the source:

```{julia}
base = runs(5; years=300)
trees, wood = column(base, :trees), column(base, :mass)
p1 = plot(0:300, trees; color=1, alpha=0.6, label="", xlabel="year", ylabel="trees")
p2 = plot(0:300, wood; color=2, alpha=0.6, label="", xlabel="year", ylabel="wood (t)")
plot(p1, p2; layout=(1, 2), size=(750, 300), left_margin=5Plots.mm, bottom_margin=5Plots.mm)
```

```{julia}
(trees_250=round(Int, mean(trees[251, :])), trees_300=round(Int, mean(trees[301, :])),
 wood_250=round(Int, mean(wood[251, :])),
 growth=round(mean(bark_beetle_growth_rate(wood[:, k]) for k in 1:5); digits=2))
```

The tree count matches the source's: about 10 100 trees from year 250, against
its 9900 to 9700. The wood does not. The source's forest carries about
21 000 t at year 240, 2.1 t a tree, and grows by 2.67% a year between years
50 and 200; here it carries about 14 200 t, 1.4 t a tree, and grows by 2.3%.
With the stated mortality, a forest in which young trees keep replacing old
ones averages 1.4 t a tree. Heavier trees need a forest of older trees than
the source's rules, as written, produce.

```{julia}
_, snaps = forest(problem(:bark_beetle_forest; seed=1, years=200); maps=(50, 100, 200))
function block_age(a; b=10)
    m = fill(NaN, size(a) .÷ b)
    for I in CartesianIndices(m)
        block = a[((I[1] - 1) * b + 1):(I[1] * b), ((I[2] - 1) * b + 1):(I[2] * b)]
        any(>(0), block) && (m[I] = mean(filter(>(0), block)))
    end
    return m
end
plot([heatmap(block_age(snaps[y]); aspect_ratio=1, c=:viridis, clims=(0, 120),
              xticks=false, yticks=false, title="year $y", titlefontsize=10,
              colorbar=true) for y in (50, 100, 200)]...;
     layout=(1, 3), size=(900, 260))
```

Each square is the mean age of the trees in a 10 × 10 m block, blank where
there are none. The forest spreads outwards from the centre, with its
youngest trees at the edge.

## Contaminated ground

In the source's second scenario, trees older than 3 die on a contaminated
patch of 30 × 60 m off the centre. Five runs:

```{julia}
contam = runs(5; years=300, contamination=true)
(trees_150=round.(Int, (mean(trees[151, :]), mean(column(contam, :trees)[151, :]))),
 trees_300=round.(Int, (mean(trees[301, :]), mean(column(contam, :trees)[301, :]))),
 wood_300=round.(Int, (mean(wood[301, :]), mean(column(contam, :mass)[301, :]))))
```

Each pair is without and with contamination. As in the source, the patch slows
the forest's spread from the centre and leaves it with slightly fewer trees and
less wood.

## Strip harvest

From year 101 to 250, the forest is cut in ten strips of 30 m, one a year in
turn, felling every tree older than 90:

```{julia}
harv = runs(5; years=250, harvest=true)
felled = column(harv, :felled)
plot(101:250, felled[102:251, 1]; lw=1.5, xlabel="year", ylabel="wood felled (t)",
     label="one run", size=(650, 300))
```

```{julia}
(mean_101_250=round(mean(felled[102:251, :]); digits=1),
 mean_196_250=round(mean(felled[197:251, :]); digits=1))
```

The yield follows the ten-year cycle of the strips and grows as the forest
fills, as in the source. It is about half the source's (116.1 t a year over the
150 years, 188.3 t once the forest is full), as its trees carry more wood.

## Drought

Droughts of ten years start after years 50 and 250. In a drought, mortality is
1.2 times its usual value, trees grow half as fast, and saplings are half as
likely. Five runs of 350 years:

```{julia}
dry = runs(5; years=350, droughts=(50, 250))
dt, dw = column(dry, :trees), column(dry, :mass)
p1 = plot(0:350, dt; color=1, alpha=0.6, label="", xlabel="year", ylabel="trees")
vspan!(p1, [50, 60, 250, 260]; color=:gray, alpha=0.2, label="drought")
p2 = plot(0:350, dw; color=2, alpha=0.6, label="", xlabel="year", ylabel="wood (t)")
vspan!(p2, [50, 60, 250, 260]; color=:gray, alpha=0.2, label="")
plot(p1, p2; layout=(1, 2), size=(750, 300), left_margin=5Plots.mm, bottom_margin=5Plots.mm)
```

```{julia}
change(x, a, b) = round(100 * (mean(x[b + 1, :]) / mean(x[a + 1, :]) - 1); digits=1)
(trees_250_to_260=change(dt, 250, 260), wood_250_to_260=change(dw, 250, 260),
 wood_250_to_350=change(dw, 250, 350))
```

These are percentage changes. As in the source, the early drought hardly
matters, while the later one costs the full forest trees and wood: here 5% of
the trees and 8% of the wood, against about 9% and 12% in the source. The
trees return within a few years, as saplings fill the gaps, but the wood is
still 3% short a century later, as the source's takes more than a century to
recover.

## Bark beetles

The source brings 2000 beetles into a 20 × 20 m patch off the centre (100
draws of 20 beetles on the trees standing there) in a year between 30 and 70,
and follows the forest for 350 years. Three runs for each year:

```{julia}
years_in = 30:5:70
outbreaks = Dict(y => runs(3; years=350, infestation=y) for y in years_in)
summary = [(year=y, run=k, before=r[y + 1].trees,
            after=minimum(getfield.(r[(y + 1):(y + 20)], :trees)),
            last=something(findlast(x -> x.infested > 0, r), 0) - 1, at250=r[251].trees)
           for y in years_in for (k, r) in enumerate(outbreaks[y])]
foreach(println, summary)
```

`before` is the forest when the beetles arrive, `after` its smallest size in
the next 20 years, `last` the last year with beetles (−1 if they found no
tree), and `at250` the forest at year 250. Where beetles find trees, they kill nearly all of the young
forest within two to four years, leaving at most about 80 trees, and then die out,
having no trees left within reach. The survivors regrow it, about as many trees by year 250 as
without beetles in most runs. Whether beetles find trees in their patch
depends on how far the forest has spread by then: in some runs it reaches the
patch before year 40, the source's first outbreak, and in others not until
year 55.

```{julia}
plot(0:300, trees[:, 1]; color=:black, lw=2, label="no beetles", xlims=(0, 350))
for (k, y) in enumerate((40, 50, 60, 70))
    plot!(0:350, getfield.(outbreaks[y][1], :trees); color=k, lw=1.2,
          label="beetles in year $y")
end
plot!(xlabel="year", ylabel="trees", legend=:bottomright, size=(650, 360))
```

Each outbreak sets the forest back by one to four decades, depending less on
when the beetles arrive than on how many trees survive them. The source's
outbreaks set it back by about ten to thirty years. The source also finds
that the forest overshoots about 200 years after an outbreak, as the cohort
that regrew, being of one age, passes 150 and dies off together. Regrown
here from tens of scattered trees over decades, the forest is not of one
age, and shows no overshoot.

How beetles move determines this. When they kill every tree they reach in a
year, they die with it; they persist only where they are spread thinly over
many neighbours, leaving some trees below 200 at the end of the year. In the
source's words, "the outbreak only occurs if the trees have enough neighbors".
